jsonld.description: Chtitha djej is Algeria's fierce chicken: the bird marinated in a dried-chile and garlic paste — the felfla row that runs from the #101 filfel chuma's family — then cooked in its own paste's red oil with a little water, until the sauce runs dark and the chicken's skin takes the chili's stain. The Maghreb's western neighbors run the m'qualli's saffron-quiet (#31); Algeria's east runs the chtitha's fire — the same chicken, the same pot, an entirely different weather.

6 cloves garlic (about 25 g), pounded to a paste with 1 tsp salt
1 tbsp sweet paprika (about 8 g); 1 tsp cumin; ½ tsp caraway (the Algerian note); black pepper
3 tbsp neutral oil (about 40 g); 150 ml water (about 150 g)
1 onion (about 150 g), grated — optional, the thinner-school's concession
To finish: a fist of cilantro (about 15 g), the juice of ½ a lemon; olives or the #104 pickled turnips beside

recipeInstructions.text: The red-oil pot (40 minutes). Warm the oil in the tagine or wide pot; add the chicken pieces with all their marinade, turning to sizzle in the oil 4 minutes. Chtitha Djej

Algerian · Easy · Serves 4

Jump to Recipe Method Troubleshooting Storage
Chtitha djej is Algeria's fierce chicken: the bird marinated in a dried-chile and garlic paste — the felfla row that runs from the #101 filfel chuma's family — then cooked in its own paste's red oil with a little water, until the sauce runs dark and the chicken's skin takes the chili's stain. The Maghreb's western neighbors run the m'qualli's saffron-quiet (#31); Algeria's east runs the chtitha's fire — the same chicken, the same pot, an entirely different weather.

Quantities live in the recipe card.

Ingredients

  • optional, the thinner-school's concession
- **Make the paste first and let it sit 10 minutes.** The rehydrated chilies, garlic, paprika, cumin, and caraway pounded together — or the flakes steeped in 3 tbsp hot water to a paste — the rest lets the flakes' bitterness soften and the flavors marry. The chile level is the cook's honest dial: four tablespoons of moderate flakes run a firm warmth; the Algerian original runs hotter. - **The bridge:** the felfla paste is this dish's own — a good harissa (#91) thinned with garlic and caraway bridges truly at a fermented register (the #101 filfel chuma is the closest cousin). The chicken: bone-in pieces, the skin left on to take the stain.

Chtitha Djej

Prep: 25 minutes, plus 1 hour marinating · Cook: 50 minutes · Total: About 2 hours 15 minutes · Serves 4

Ingredients

Ingredients

  • 1 chicken (about 1.3 kg), cut to 8 pieces
  • 4 tbsp dried red chile flakes or 6 rehydrated dried chilies, blended to a paste with a splash of their soak water (about 20 g flakes)
  • 6 cloves garlic (about 25 g), pounded to a paste with 1 tsp salt
  • 1 tbsp sweet paprika (about 8 g); 1 tsp cumin; ½ tsp caraway (the Algerian note); black pepper
  • 3 tbsp neutral oil (about 40 g); 150 ml water (about 150 g)
  • 1 onion (about 150 g), grated — optional, the thinner-school's concession
  • To finish: a fist of cilantro (about 15 g), the juice of ½ a lemon; olives or the #104 pickled turnips beside

Instructions

  1. **Marinate (1 hour).** Coat the chicken pieces thoroughly in the paste (reserving a spoonful for the pot's finish) with half the garlic; rest, covered, in the refrigerator 1 hour. Checkpoint — the chicken's skin should be visibly stained red-orange, the paste clinging in the creases — the stain is the dish's visual signature, and the marinade's hour drives the fire inward.
  2. **The red-oil pot (40 minutes).** Warm the oil in the tagine or wide pot; add the chicken pieces with all their marinade, turning to sizzle in the oil 4 minutes. The water poured down the side, the reserved paste stirred in, the onion if running — cover, adjust to the barest tremble (95 °C), and cook 35–40 minutes, turning once, until the chicken is tender to the bone and the sauce has reduced to a dark, red-gold, intensely flavored coat that clings heavily to each piece. Checkpoint — the sauce's end: not a broth but a lacquer's worth — the pot's bottom holding barely a spoonable film of dark red oil and concentrated chile, the chicken's surface glossy with it. Taste: fierce first, garlic behind, cumin's earth and caraway's anise — the salt one notch past comfort, for the bread will carry.
  3. **The finish and the service.** Off the flame: the lemon's juice through, the cilantro over, and the pot rested 5 minutes — served with bread and the sharp pickles that the fire demands. Checkpoint — eating test, with bread: the chicken's stained skin lacquered with the chile-garlic oil, the meat within carrying the paste's fire and the caraway's whisper — the lemon's lift at each swallow, the bread's cool chew between, and a pickle's cut when the fire needs it. It should be a sweating, alive dish — the eastern Maghreb's own register, and completely its own weather against the #31's saffron.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Sauce bitterFlakes over-toasted or paste burnt at the sizzleThe paste's rest; the sizzle's 4 minutes watched
Dish all heat, no depthGarlic or caraway shyThe garlic leads the fire \u2014 six cloves' honest measure
Sauce thin, poolsWater over-measuredThe 150 ml splash \u2014 the lacquer is the goal

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

- Keeps 3 days refrigerated and deepens (the fire mellowing into the meat); the reheat is a covered whisper of a simmer. The paste batch keeps a week refrigerated for the next pot. - Variations: the lamb chtitha, the chickpea version. The #101 filfel chuma is this paste's own record; the #88 loubia b'dersa is the same fire in the bean canon.
